dedupe_keys.name: storm arwen review final report energy emergencies executive committee june 2022

description: This case study is the final report of the Energy Emergencies Executive Committee review of Storm Arwen, commissioned by the UK Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy in December 2021 and published in June 2022 (38 pages). It covers how the distribution and transmission network operators fared in Storm Arwen of November 2021 and, for comparison, Storm Eunice of February 2022 when 1.7 million households lost supply for over three minutes. Charts break down customers and faults by voltage level, for example 9,741 faults and about 1.12 million customers affected in Arwen with 83% of customers hit by high voltage faults, and the report concludes that wind and falling trees caused most damage. Its actions address system resilience, consumer protection including call centres and compensation, and additional support for local resilience partners. Access: free PDF under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Coverage is the electricity distribution networks of Great Britain. Caveats: only the executive summary, introduction and resilience section were read here, and figures rely on operator-supplied data. It suits resilience and emergency response studies of overhead distribution networks, and no directly related records are catalogued yet.

organisations: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
outcomes: The review found that existing network standards did not give adequate resilience to a northerly wind with sustained high speeds, snow and ice. By fault type, 934,942 customers (83%) were affected by high voltage faults, 161,578 (15%) by extra high voltage faults and 26,752 (2%) by low voltage faults, from 9,741 faults; damage came mainly from wind and falling trees. It recommends actions on physical resilience standards, storm planning, repair and restoration tools, the NEWSAC mutual aid forum, customer call centres, compensation and support for local resilience partners.
